_how: The editor writes one piece a day: stories on even days, spices on odd days, from the top of each list, then moves it to done with the date. Jacqueline or the editor may add, reorder or cut. Recipes are never written by the editor: they go to recipes_for_zahra.

stories.angle: The pause after the long lunch: shutters half closed, the house slows, tea again. Why the middle of the day belongs to rest. Blends: dusk, a-whole-day.
The couscoussier and the gsaa: who makes the clay and wooden tools of couscous (UNESCO names potters and family workshops), and why a dish needs its own pot. Blends: ras-el-hanout.
The white cone of sugar: the little hammer, the lidded box, two loaves carried to a marriage proposal, and Morocco's Saadian sugar mills of the sixteenth century. Blends: sweet-tagine, spiced-coffee.
The attar of Souk el-Attarine: one seller for scent and spice together, rose buds beside cloves, amber beside cinnamon; the word that gave English attar of roses. Blends: ras-el-hanout, dusk.
Khlii: strips of meat rubbed with garlic, cumin and coriander, dried in the sun on medina roofs, kept under fat, fried with eggs on a winter morning. Blends: kemoun, chermoula.

Hand washing at the table: the brass kettle and basin carried round before and after the meal, the towel. Penn Museum holds a Moroccan kettle and basin from the 1898 Williams expedition, noted as used to wash hands at meals. Blends: dusk, sweet-tagine.

The nafar: the Ramadan horn player who walks the old medina at 3am to wake people for the pre-dawn meal, thanked with sugar and coins, now rare outside the old cities (Africanews 2024). Blends: spiced-coffee, golden-hour.
The wardrobe-sized msemen and harcha shops of the medina, usually run by women, a coin or two a square, honey and butter or khlii inside. Blends: golden-hour, kemoun.
Kaab el ghazal: the almond and rosewater crescents relatives bake weeks before a wedding, and the Almohad-era dough with anise (Yabiladi, 2025). Blends: sweet-tagine.

spices.angle: Elbezar: the pepper that travelled the caravan routes, in nearly every Moroccan blend. Blends: golden-hour, ras-el-hanout.
Gouza and bsibsa: one fruit, two spices, sweet tagines and ras el hanout. Blends: sweet-tagine, spiced-coffee, ras-el-hanout.
White pepper beside the black: the softer heat in a pale chicken tagine with olives and lemon, no dark flecks in the sauce. Blends: golden-hour, ras-el-hanout.
Karwiya: the seed in harissa, cousin of cumin and often mistaken for it. Blends: dry-harissa.
Qronfel: the nail-shaped bud in ras el hanout and spiced coffee, and the Moluccan islands it came from. Blends: spiced-coffee, ras-el-hanout.
Origanum compactum, the other zaatar of the Middle Atlas and the Rif, now also grown by cooperatives near Khenifra; how it differs from thyme in the pot. Blends: moroccan-zaatar.
Zhar: bitter orange flowers distilled into the water sprinkled on guests and stirred into pastries and tea. Blends: dusk.
